fields.category: American persimmon cultivars for northern areas

rows.name: Early Golden
rows.harvest_time: late September through October at Urbana, Illinois
rows.description: McDaniel says Early Golden was selected about 1880 by E. A. Riehl near Alton, Illinois, and was the oldest American persimmon cultivar still propagated. The article says it excels most wild persimmons in fruit size, firmness, and earliness, and is adapted through USDA Zone 5

rows.name: Garretson
rows.description: McDaniel describes Garretson as a Pennsylvania introduction and close descendant of Early Golden. At Geneva, New York, it matured more fully than Early Golden in most years, while at Urbana its fruit was a little smaller than Early Golden but preferred by most tasters for flavor and texture

rows.name: Killen
rows.harvest_time: starts ripening nearly as early as Early Golden and often hangs later
rows.description: McDaniel says Killen was raised from Early Golden seed by Joseph Killen of Felton, Delaware. The article says it had been thought to have D. kaki as a pollen parent but showed no evidence of species hybridity, and that it averaged slightly larger than Early Golden

rows.name: Florence
rows.description: McDaniel describes Florence as an Urbana selection by Herbert C. Barrett and J. C. McDaniel from open-pollinated Killen seed, probably with William as the pollen parent. The article says it compared favorably with Garretson for flavor and texture, had the smallest seeds of the group, and sometimes bore male flowers

rows.name: John Rick
rows.description: McDaniel describes John Rick as an Urbana selection, probably Killen x William. The article says fruit up to two inches was larger than Early Golden, attractive, desirable for fresh fruit sales, similar in flavor and texture to Early Golden, and less likely to puncture packaged fruit because of a smaller, softer calyx

rows.name: California
rows.description: McDaniel says California originated in California, probably as a seedling of Early Golden, and was named by Harvey Steele after being grafted at Reading, Pennsylvania. The article says it did well at Linton, Indiana, and strongly resembled Early Golden there, although smaller and more rounded

rows.name: Wabash
rows.harvest_time: opens the Urbana season by mid-August and generally ends in September
rows.description: McDaniel says Wabash was selected wild near Pinkstaff in Lawrence County, Illinois. The article describes seedless fruit when pollinated by nearby 60-chromosome males, smaller fruit than the preceding cultivars, deep red-orange color, sweet aromatic flavor, and red-pigmented fall foliage

rows.name: Craggs
rows.harvest_time: October to November at Urbana, Illinois
rows.description: McDaniel says Craggs was selected wild near Harrisburg, Illinois. The article notes red autumn foliage and red-blushed fruit skin over light yellow flesh, with fruit slightly smaller than John Rick and very good for fresh eating, though softer and harder to market than John Rick or Early Golden

rows.name: Meader
rows.description: McDaniel says the name Meader was suggested for N.H.-P 1, a seedling of Garretson by E. M. Meader in New Hampshire. The article says it produced large crops of mostly seedless fruit, sometimes produced staminate flowers, and was reported as very prolific at Geneva, New York

rows.name: Marion
rows.description: McDaniel says Marion is probably the correct name for a large, fairly late persimmon often propagated as Miller. The article says it was less attractive and less flavorful than several other cultivars, but very productive and useful for fruit and pulp in USDA Zone 6b or southward

rows.name: Miller
rows.description: McDaniel says Miller was cultivated at Urbana and in southeastern Pennsylvania and was one of Fayette Etter's favorite market varieties. The article describes pleasant flavor, less sugar than other persimmons of its season, and fruit smaller and finer textured than Marion

rows.name: Beaver
rows.description: McDaniel describes Beaver as a small-fruited persimmon from near Mitchell, Indiana, notable as the ingredient in several prize-winning persimmon puddings

rows.name: Penland
rows.description: McDaniel says Penland originated as an isolated clone in the Blue Ridge Mountains of North Carolina and was hardy at Urbana. The article says it was introduced as seedless but set seeds when pollinated by 60-chromosome males, with fruit smaller and less sweet than Wabash

rows.name: Knowles
rows.description: McDaniel says Knowles showed a high degree of seedlessness when pollinated by males of both chromosome races, and that the original tree in Gibson County, Indiana, had a trunk circumference over 13 feet. The article found its fruit too small, soft, and late for value at Urbana, but possibly interesting farther south

rows.name: Festimoon
rows.description: McDaniel says Festimoon originated near Mitchell, Indiana, and was consistently seedless there. The article describes fruit larger and firmer than Knowles and ripening earlier in October, but not as sweet as most cultivars

fields.category: Staminate American persimmon pollenizer for northern areas

rows.name: William
rows.description: McDaniel describes William as a staminate selection made at Urbana that produced abundant staminate flowers over a rather long season, useful as a pollenizer for persimmon plantings
